\noindent \textsuperscript{58} And I said unto them, Both ye are holy unto the Lord, and the vessels are holy, and the gold and the silver is a vow unto the Lord, the Lord of our fathers. \textsuperscript{59} Watch ye, and keep them till ye deliver them to the chief of the priests and Levites, and to the principal men of the families of Israel, in Jerusalem, into the chambers of the house of our God. \textsuperscript{60} So the priests and the Levites, who had received the silver and the gold and the vessels that were in Jerusalem, brought them into the temple of the Lord.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{61} And from the river Theras we departed the twelfth day of the first month, and came to Jerusalem by the mighty hand of our Lord, which was with us: and from the beginning of our journey the Lord delivered us from every enemy, and so we came to Jerusalem. \textsuperscript{62} And when we had been there three days, the gold and silver that was weighed was delivered in the house of our Lord on the fourth day unto Marmothi the priest the son of Uria. \textsuperscript{63} And with him was Eleazar the son of Phinees, and with them were Josabad the son of Jesu and Moeth the son of Sabban, Levites: all was delivered them by number and weight. \textsuperscript{64} And all the weight of them was written up the same hour.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{65} Moreover they that were come out of the captivity offered sacrifice unto the Lord God of Israel, even twelve bullocks for all Israel, fourscore and sixteen rams, \textsuperscript{66} threescore and twelve lambs, goats for a peace-offering, twelve; all of them a sacrifice to the Lord. \textsuperscript{67} And they delivered the king's commandments unto the king's stewards, and to the governors of Celosyria and Phenice; and they honoured the people and the temple of God.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{68} Now when these things were done, the rulers came unto me, and said, \textsuperscript{69} The nation of Israel, the princes, the priests and the Levites, have not put away from them the strange people of the land, nor their pollutions from the Gentiles, to wit , the Canaanites, Hittites, Pheresites, Jebusites, and the Moabites, Egyptians, and Edomites. \textsuperscript{70} For both they and their sons have married with their daughters, and the holy seed is mixed with the strange people of the land; and from the beginning of this matter the rulers and the great men have been partakers of this iniquity.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{71} And as soon as I had heard these things, I rent my clothes, and the holy garment, and pulled off the hair from off my head and beard, and sat me down sad and very heavy. \textsuperscript{72} So all they that were then moved at the word of the Lord God of Israel assembled unto me, whilst I mourned for the iniquity: but I sat still full of heaviness until the evening sacrifice.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{73} Then rising up from the fast with my clothes and the holy garment rent, and bowing my knees, and stretching forth my hands unto the Lord, \textsuperscript{74} I said, O Lord, I am confounded and ashamed before thy face; \textsuperscript{75} for our sins are multiplied above our heads, and our ignorances have reached up unto heaven. \textsuperscript{76} For ever since the time of our fathers we have been and are in great sin, even unto this day. \textsuperscript{77} And for our sins and our fathers' we with our brethren and our kings and our priests were given up unto the kings of the earth, to the sword, and to captivity, and for a prey with shame, unto this day.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{78} And now in some measure hath mercy been shewed unto us from thee, O Lord, that there should be left us a root and a name in the place of thy sanctuary; \textsuperscript{79} and to discover unto us a light in the house of the Lord our God, and to give us food in the time of our servitude. \textsuperscript{80} Yea, when we were in bondage, we were not forsaken of our Lord; but he made us favoured before the kings of Persia, so that they gave us food; \textsuperscript{81} yea, and honoured the temple of our Lord, and raised up the desolate Sion, so that they have given us a sure abiding in Jewry and Jerusalem.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{82} And now, O Lord, what shall we say, having these things? for we have transgressed thy commandments, which thou gavest by the hand of thy servants the prophets, saying, \textsuperscript{83} That the land, which ye enter into to possess as an heritage, is a land polluted with the pollutions of the strangers of the land, and they have filled it with their uncleanness. \textsuperscript{84} Therefore now shall ye not join your daughters unto their sons, neither shall ye take their daughters unto your sons. \textsuperscript{85} Moreover ye shall never seek to have peace with them, that ye may be strong, and eat the good things of the land, and that ye may leave the inheritance of the land unto your children for evermore.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{86} And all that is befallen is done unto us for our wicked works and great sins: for thou, O Lord, didst make our sins light, \textsuperscript{87} and didst give unto us such a root: but we have turned back again to transgress thy law, and to mingle ourselves with the uncleanness of the nations of the land. \textsuperscript{88} Mightest not thou be angry with us to destroy us, till thou hadst left us neither root, seed, nor name?\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{89} O Lord of Israel, thou art true: for we are left a root this day. \textsuperscript{90} Behold, now are we before thee in our iniquities, for we cannot stand any longer by reason of these things before thee. \textsuperscript{91} And as Esdras in his prayer made his confession, weeping, and lying flat upon the ground before the temple, there gathered unto him from Jerusalem a very great multitude of men and women and children: for there was great weeping among the multitude.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{92} Then Jechonias the son of Jeelus, one of the children of Israel, called out and said, O Esdras, we have sinned against the Lord; we have married strange women of the nations of the land, and now is all Israel aloft. \textsuperscript{93} Let us make an oath to the Lord, that we will put away all our wives, which we have taken of the heathen, with their children, \textsuperscript{94} like as thou hast decreed, and as many as do obey the law of the Lord. \textsuperscript{95} Arise, and put into execution: for to thee doth this matter appertain, and we will be with thee: do valiantly. \textsuperscript{96} So Esdras arose, and took an oath of the chief of the priests and Levites of all Israel to do after these things; and so they sware.\par
\subsection*{Esdras I 9}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} Then Esdras rising from the court of the temple went to the chamber of Joanan the son of Eliasib, \textsuperscript{2} and remained there, and did eat no meat nor drink water, mourning for the great iniquities of the multitude. \textsuperscript{3} And there was a proclamation in all Jewry and Jerusalem to all them that were of the captivity, that they should be gathered together at Jerusalem: \textsuperscript{4} and that whosoever met not there within two or three days, according as the elders that bare rule appointed, their cattle should be seized to the use of the temple, and himself cast out from them that were of the captivity.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{5} And in three days were all they of the tribe of Juda and Benjamin gathered together at Jerusalem the twentieth day of the ninth month. \textsuperscript{6} And all the multitude sat in the broad court of the temple, trembling because of the present foul weather.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{7} So Esdras arose up, and said unto them, Ye have transgressed the law in marrying strange wives, thereby to increase the sins of Israel. \textsuperscript{8} And now by confessing give glory unto the Lord God of our fathers, \textsuperscript{9} and do his will, and separate yourselves from the heathen of the land, and from the strange women.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{10} Then cried the whole multitude, and said with a loud voice, Like as thou hast spoken, so will we do. \textsuperscript{11} But forasmuch as the people are many, and it is foul weather, so that we cannot stand without, and this is not a work of a day or two, seeing our sin in these things is spread far: \textsuperscript{12} therefore let the rulers of the multitude stay, and let all them of our habitations that have strange wives come at the time appointed, \textsuperscript{13} and with them the rulers and judges of every place, till we turn away the wrath of the Lord from us for this matter.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{14} Then Jonathan the son of Azael and Ezechias the son of Theocanus accordingly took this matter upon them: and Mosollam and Levis and Sabbatheus helped them. \textsuperscript{15} And they that were of the captivity did according to all these things. \textsuperscript{16} And Esdras the priest chose unto him the principal men of their families, all by name: and in the first day of the tenth month they sat together to examine the matter. \textsuperscript{17} So their cause that held strange wives was brought to an end in the first day of the first month.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{18} And of the priests that were come together, and had strange wives, there were found; \textsuperscript{19} of the sons of Jesus the son of Josedec, and his brethren; Matthelas, and Eleazar, and Joribus, and Joadanus. \textsuperscript{20} And they gave their hands to put away their wives, and to offer rams to make reconcilement for their errors.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{21} And of the sons of Emmer: Ananias, and Zabdeus, and Manes, and Samæus, and Hiereel, and Azarias. \textsuperscript{22} And of the sons of Phaisur; Elionais, Massias, Ismael, and Nathanael, and Ocodelus, and Saloas.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{23} And of the Levites; Jozabad, and Semis, and Coïus, who was called Calitas, and Patheus, and Judas, and Jonas. \textsuperscript{24} Of the holy singers: Eleasabus, Bacchurus. \textsuperscript{25} Of the porters; Salumus, and Tolbanes.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{26} Of them of Israel, of the sons of Phoros; Hiermas, and Jezias, and Melchias, and Maelus, and Eleazar, and Asebias, and Banæas. \textsuperscript{27} Of the sons of Ela; Matthanias, Zacharias, and Jezrielus, and Joabdius, and Hieremoth, and Aïdias. \textsuperscript{28} And of the sons of Zamoth; Eliadas, Eliasimus, Othonias, Jarimoth, and Sabatus, and Zeralias. \textsuperscript{29} Of the sons of Bebai; Joannes, and Ananias, and Josabad, and Amatheis. \textsuperscript{30} Of the sons of Mani; Olamus, Mamuchus, Jedeus, Jasubus, Jasael, and Hieremoth. \textsuperscript{31} And of the sons of Addi; Naathus, and Moosias, Lacunus, and Naidus, Matthanias, and Sesthel, Balnuus, and Manasseas. \textsuperscript{32} And of the sons of Annas; Elionas, and Asaias, and Melchias, and Sabbeus, and Simon Chosameus. \textsuperscript{33} And of the sons of Asom; Altaneus, and Mattathias, and Sabanneus, Eliphalat, and Manasses, and Semei. \textsuperscript{34} And of the sons of Baani: Jeremias, Momdis, Ismaerus, Juel, Mabdai, and Pedias, and Anos, Rabasion, and Enasibus, and Mamnitanaimus, Eliasis, Bannus, Eliali, Samis, Selemias, Nathanias: and of the sons of Ezora; Sesis, Esril, Azaelus, Samatus, Zambri, Josephus. \textsuperscript{35} And of the sons of Ethma; Mazitias, Zabadaias, Edaïs, Juel, Banaias.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{36} All these had taken strange wives, and they put them away with their children.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{37} And the priests and Levites, and they that were of Israel, dwelt in Jerusalem, and in the country, in the first day of the seventh month: so the children of Israel were in their habitations.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{38} And the whole multitude came together with one accord into the broad place of the holy porch toward the east: \textsuperscript{39} and they spake unto Esdras the priest and reader, that he would bring the law of Moses, that was given of the Lord God of Israel. \textsuperscript{40} So Esdras the chief priest brought the law to the whole multitude from man to woman, and to all the priests, to hear the law in the first day of the seventh month. \textsuperscript{41} And he read in the broad court before the holy porch from morning unto midday, before both men and women; and all the multitude gave heed unto the law.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{42} And Esdras the priest and reader of the law stood up upon a pulpit of wood which was made for that purpose . \textsuperscript{43} And there stood up by him Mattathias, Sammus, Ananias, Azarias, Urias, Ezecias, Baalsamus, upon the right hand: \textsuperscript{44} and upon his left hand Phaldaius, and Misael, Melchias, Lothasubus, Nabarias, Zacharias.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{45} Then took Esdras the book of the law before the multitude: for he sat honourably in the first place in the sight of them all. \textsuperscript{46} And when he opened the law, they stood all straight up. So Esdras blessed the Lord God most High, the God of hosts, Almighty. \textsuperscript{47} And all the people answered, Amen; and lifting up their hands they fell to the ground, and worshipped the Lord.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{48} Also Jesus, Anniuth, Sarabias, Adinus, Jacubus, Sabateas, Auteas, Maiannas, and Calitas, Azarias, and Joazabdus, and Ananias, Phalias, the Levites, taught the law of the Lord, and read the law of the Lord to the multitude, making them withal to understand it.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{49} Then spake Attharates unto Esdras the chief priest and reader, and to the Levites that taught the multitude, even to all, saying, \textsuperscript{50} This day is holy unto the Lord; (for they all wept when they heard the law:) \textsuperscript{51} go then, and eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send part to them that have nothing: \textsuperscript{52} for this day is holy unto the Lord: and be not sorrowful; for the Lord will bring you to honour.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{53} So the Levites published all things to the people, saying, This day is holy to the Lord; be not sorrowful. \textsuperscript{54} Then went they their way, every one to eat and drink and make merry, and to give part to them that had nothing, and to make great cheer; \textsuperscript{55} because they understood the words wherein they were instructed, and for the which they had been assembled.\par
\section*{The Prayer of Manasses}
\subsection*{The Prayer of Manasses 1}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} O Lord Almighty, the God of our fathers Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and of their righteous seed; \textsuperscript{2} that hast made the heaven and the earth with all their adornment; \textsuperscript{3} that hast bound the sea with the word of thy commandment; that hast closed the abyss and sealed it with thy fearful and glorious name; \textsuperscript{4} whom all things revere and tremble before the face of thy power, \textsuperscript{5} because the magnificence of thy glory is unendurable and irresistible the wrath of thy threatening against sinners: \textsuperscript{6} the mercy of thy promise is both immeasurable and inscrutable; \textsuperscript{7} for thou art the Lord most high, compassionate, longsuffering, and most merciful, repenting of the evils of men. Thou, Lord, according to the abundance of thy goodness, hast proclaimed repentance and forgiveness to those that have sinned against thee, and in the multitude of thy kindnesses thou hast decreed for sinners repentance unto salvation. \textsuperscript{8} Surely thou, O Lord, the God of the just, hast not appointed repentance for the just, for Abraham and Isaac and Jacob who have not sinned against thee; but thou hast appointed repentance for me a sinner: \textsuperscript{9} for I have sinned above the number of the sand of the sea. My transgressions are multiplied, O Lord, they are multiplied, and I am not worthy to look at or see the height of heaven, for the multitude of my iniquities, \textsuperscript{10} being bowed down by many iron bonds, so that I cannot uplift my head, and there is no release for me, because I have provoked thy anger, and have done evil before thee, not doing thy will, nor keeping thy commandments, but setting up abominations and multiplying offences. \textsuperscript{11} And now I bend the knee of my heart, beseeching thy goodness: \textsuperscript{12} I have sinned, Lord, I have sinned, and I acknowledge my transgressions: \textsuperscript{13} but I pray and beseech thee, release me, Lord, release me, and destroy me not with my transgressions; keep not evils for me in anger for ever, nor condemn me to the lowest parts of the earth: because thou art God, the God of the repenting; \textsuperscript{14} and in me thou wilt shew all thy benevolence, for that me unworthy thou wilt save, according to thy great mercy: \textsuperscript{15} and I will praise thee continually all the days of my life: for all the host of the heavens sings to thee, and thine is the glory for ever and ever. Amen.\par
\section*{Maccabees III}
\subsection*{Maccabees III 1}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} Now Philopater, on learning from those who came back that Antiochus had made himself master of the places which belonged to himself, sent orders to all his footmen and horsemen, took with him his sister Arsinoe, and marched out as far as the parts of Raphia, where Antiochus and his forces encamped.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{2} And one Theodotus, intending to carry out his design, took with him the bravest of the armed men who had been before committed to his trust by Ptolemy, and got through at night to the tent of Ptolemy, to kill him on his own responsibility, and so to end the war. \textsuperscript{3} But Dositheus, called the son of Drimulus, by birth a Jew, afterward a renegade from the laws and observances of his country, conveyed Ptolemy away, and made an obscure person lie down in his stead in the tent. It befel this man to receive the fate which was meant for the other.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{4} A fierce battle then took place; and the men of Antiochus prevailing, Arsinoe continually went up and down the ranks, and with dishevelled hair, with tears and entreaties, begged the soldiers to fight manfully for themselves, their children, and wives; and promised that if they proved conquerors, she would give them two minæ of gold apiece. \textsuperscript{5} It thus fell out that their enemies were defeated in hand-to-hand encounter, and that many of them were taken prisoners.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{6} Having vanquished this attempt, the king then decided to proceed to the neighbouring cities, and encourage them. \textsuperscript{7} By doing this, and by making donations to their temples, he inspired his subjects with confidence. \textsuperscript{8} The Jews also sent some of their council and of their elders to him. The greetings, guest-gifts, and congratulations on the past, bestowed by them, filled him with the greater eagerness to visit their city.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{9} Having arrived at Jerusalem, sacrificed, and offered thank-offerings to the Greatest God, and done whatever else was suitable to the sanctity of the place, and entered the inner court, \textsuperscript{10} he was so struck with the exact magnificence of the place, and so wondered at the orderly arrangements of the temple, that he conceived the purpose of entering the sanctuary itself.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{11} And when they told him that this was not permissible, none of the nation, no, nor even the priests in general, but only the supreme high priest of all, and he only once in a year, being allowed to go in, he would by no means give way. \textsuperscript{12} Then they read the law to him; but he persisted in obtruding himself, exclaiming, that he ought to be allowed: and saying, Be it that they were deprived of this honour, I ought not to be. \textsuperscript{13} And he put the question, Why, when he entered all temples, none of the priests who were present forbad him?\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{14} He was thoughtlessly answered by some one, That he did wrong to boast of this. \textsuperscript{15} Well; since I have done this, said he, be the cause what it may, shall I not enter with or without your consent? \textsuperscript{16} And when the priests fell down in their sacred vestments imploring the Greatest God to come and help in time of need, and to avert the violence of the fierce aggressor, and when they filled the temple with lamentations and tears, \textsuperscript{17} then those who had been left behind in the city were scared, and rushed forth, uncertain of the event.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{18} Virgins, who had been shut up within their chambers, came out with their mothers, scattering dust and ashes on their heads, and filling the streets with outcries. \textsuperscript{19} Women, but recently separated off, left their bridal chambers, left the reserve that befitted them, and ran about the city in a disorderly manner. \textsuperscript{20} Newborn babes were deserted by the mothers or nurses who waited upon them; some here, some there, in houses, or in fields; these now, with an ardour which could not be checked, swarmed into the Most High temple. \textsuperscript{21} Various were the prayers offered up by those who assembled in this place, on account of the unholy attempt of the king.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{22} Along with these there were some of the citizens who took courage, and would not submit to his obstinacy, and his intention of carrying out his purpose. \textsuperscript{23} Calling out to arms, and to die bravely in defence of the law of their fathers, they created a great uproar in the place, and were with difficulty brought back by the aged and the elders to the station of prayer which they had occupied before.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{24} During this time the multitude kept on praying. \textsuperscript{25} The elders who surrounded the king strove in many ways to divert his haughty mind from the design which he had formed. \textsuperscript{26} He, in his hardened mood, insensible to all persuasion, was going onwards, with the view of carrying out this design.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{27} Yet even his own officers, when they saw this, joined the Jews in an appeal to Him who has all power, to aid in the present crisis, and not wink at such overweening lawlessness. \textsuperscript{28} Such was the frequency and the vehemence of the cry of the assembled crowd, that an indescribable noise ensued. \textsuperscript{29} Not the men only, the very walls and floor seemed to sound forth; all things preferring dissolution rather than to see the place defiled.\par
\subsection*{Maccabees III 2}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} Now was it that the high priest Simon bowed his knees over against the holy place, and spread out his hands in reverent form, and uttered the following supplication:\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{2} O Lord, Lord, King of the heavens, and Ruler of the whole creation, Holy among the holy, sole Governor, Almighty, give ear to us who are oppressed by a wicked and profane one, who exulteth in his confidence and strength. \textsuperscript{3} It is thou, the Creator of all, the Lord of the universe, who art a righteous Governor, and judgest all who act with pride and insolence.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{4} It was thou who didst destroy the former workers of unrighteousness, among whom were the giants, who trusted in their strength and hardihood, by covering them with a measureless flood. \textsuperscript{5} It was thou who didst make the Sodomites, those workers of exceeding iniquity, men notorious for their vices, an example to after generations, when thou didst consume them with fire and brimstone.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{6} Thou didst make known thy power when thou causedst the bold Pharaoh, the enslaver of thy people, to pass through the ordeal of many and diverse inflictions. \textsuperscript{7} And thou rolledst the depths of the sea over him, when he made pursuit with chariots, and with a multitude of followers, and gavest a safe passage to those who put their trust in thee, the Lord of the whole creation. \textsuperscript{8} These saw and felt the works of thine hands, and praised thee the Almighty.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{9} Thou, O King, when thou createdst the illimitable and measureless earth, didst choose out this city: thou didst make this place sacred to thy name, albeit thou needest nothing: thou didst glorify it with thy illustrious presence, after constructing it to the glory of thy great and honourable name.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{10} And thou didst promise, out of love to the house of Israel, that should we fall away from thee, and become afflicted, and then come to this house and pray, thou wouldest hear our prayer. \textsuperscript{11} Verily thou art faithful and true.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{12} And whereas thou didst often aid our fathers when hard pressed, and in low estate, and deliveredst them out of great dangers, \textsuperscript{13} see now, holy King, how through our many and great sins we are borne down, and made subject to our enemies, and are become weak and powerless. \textsuperscript{14} We being in this low condition, this bold and profane man seeks to dishonour this thy holy place, consecrated out of the earth to the name of thy Majesty.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{15} Thy dwelling-place, the heaven of heavens, is indeed unapproachable to men. \textsuperscript{16} But since it seemed good to thee to exhibit thy glory among thy people Israel, thou didst sanctify this place. \textsuperscript{17} Punish us not by means of the uncleanness of their men, nor chastise us by means of their profanity; lest the lawless ones should boast in their rage, and exult in exuberant pride of speech, and say, \textsuperscript{18} We have trampled upon the holy house, as idolatrous houses are trampled upon.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{19} Blot out our iniquities, and do away with our errors, and shew forth thy compassion in this hour. \textsuperscript{20} Let thy mercies quickly go before us. Grant us peace, that the cast down and broken hearted may praise thee with their mouth.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{21} At that time God, who seeth all things, who is beyond all Holy among the holy, heard that prayer, so suitable; and scourged the man greatly uplifted with scorn and insolence. \textsuperscript{22} Shaking him to and fro as a reed is shaken with the wind, he cast him upon the pavement, powerless, with limbs paralyzed; by a righteous judgment deprived of the faculty of speech.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{23} His friends and body-guards, beholding the swift recompense which had suddenly overtaken him, struck with exceeding terror, and fearing that he would die, speedily removed him. \textsuperscript{24} When in course of time he had come to himself, this severe check caused no repentance within him, but he departed with bitter threatenings. \textsuperscript{25} He proceeded to Egypt, grew worse in wickedness through his beforementioned companions in wine, who were lost to all goodness; \textsuperscript{26} and not satisfied with countless acts of impiety, his audacity so increased that he raised evil reports there, and many of his friends, watching his purpose attentively, joined in furthering his will.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{27} His purpose was to inflict a public stigma upon our race; wherefore he erected a pillar at the tower-porch, and caused the following inscription to be engraven upon it: \textsuperscript{28} That entrance to their own temple was to be refused to all those who would not sacrifice; that all the Jews were to be registered among the common people; that those who resisted were to be forcibly seized and put to death; \textsuperscript{29} that those who were thus registered, were to be marked on their persons by the ivy-leaf symbol of Dionysus, and to be set apart with these limited rights.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{30} To do away with the appearance of hating them all, he had it written underneath, that if any of them should elect to enter the community of those initiated in the rites, these should have equal rights with the Alexandrians.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{31} Some of those who were over the city, therefore, abhorring any approach to the city of piety, unhesitatingly gave in to the king, and expected to derive some great honour from a future connection with him. \textsuperscript{32} A nobler spirit, however, prompted the majority to cling to their religious observances, and by paying money that they might live unmolested, these sought to escape the registration: \textsuperscript{33} cheerfully looking forward to future aid, they abhorred their own apostates, considering them to be national foes, and debarring them from the common usages of social intercourse.\par
\subsection*{Maccabees III 3}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} On discovering this, so incensed was the wicked king, that he no longer confined his rage to the Jews in Alexandria. Laying his hand more heavily upon those who lived in the country, he gave orders that they should be quickly collected into one place, and most cruelly deprived of their lives.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{2} While this was going on, an invidious rumour was uttered abroad by men who had banded together to injure the Jewish race. The purport of their charge was, that the Jews kept them away from the ordinances of the law. \textsuperscript{3} Now, while the Jews always maintained a feeling of unswerving loyalty towards the kings, \textsuperscript{4} yet, as they worshipped God, and observed his law, they made certain distinctions, and avoided certain things. Hence some persons held them in odium; \textsuperscript{5} although, as they adorned their conversation with works of righteousness, they had established themselves in the good opinion of the world.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{6} What all the rest of mankind said, was, however, made of no account by the foreigners; \textsuperscript{7} who said much of the exclusiveness of the Jews with regard to their worship and meats; they alleged that they were men unsociable, hostile to the king's interests, refusing to associate with him or his troops. By this way of speaking, they brought much odium upon them.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{8} Nor was this unexpected uproar and sudden conflux of people unobserved by the Greeks who lived in the city, concerning men who had never harmed them: yet to aid them was not in their power, since all was oppression around; but they encouraged the Jews by sympathizing with them in their troubles, and expected a favourable turn of affairs: \textsuperscript{9} He who knoweth all things, will not, said they , disregard so great a people. \textsuperscript{10} Some of the neighbours, friends, and fellow dealers of the Jews, even called them secretly to an interview, pledged them their assistance, and promised to do their very utmost for them.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{11} Now the king, elated with his prosperous fortune, and not regarding the superior power of God, but thinking to persevere in his present purpose, wrote the following letter to the prejudice of the Jews.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{12} King Ptolemy Philopater, to the commanders and soldiers in Egypt, and in all places, health and happiness! \textsuperscript{13} I am right well; and so, too, are my affairs. \textsuperscript{14} Since our Asiatic campaign, the particulars of which ye know, and which by the aid of the gods, not lightly given, and by our own vigour, has been brought to a successful issue according to our expectation, \textsuperscript{15} we resolved, not with strength of spear, but with gentleness and much humanity, as it were to nurse the inhabitants of Cœle-Syria and Phœnicia, and to be their willing benefactors.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{16} So, having bestowed considerable sums of money upon the temples of the several cities, we proceeded even as far as Jerusalem; and went up to honour the temple of these wretched beings who never cease from their folly. \textsuperscript{17} To outward appearance they received us willingly; but belied that appearance by their deeds. When we were eager to enter their temple, and to honour it with the most beautiful and exquisite gifts, \textsuperscript{18} they were so carried away by their old arrogance, as to forbid us the entrance; while we, out of our forbearance toward all men, refrained from exercising our power upon them. \textsuperscript{19} And thus, exhibiting their enmity against us, they alone among the nations lift up their heads against kings and benefactors, as men unwilling to submit to any thing reasonable.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{20} We then, having endeavoured to make allowance for the madness of these persons, and on our victorious return treating all people in Egypt courteously, acted in a manner which was befitting. \textsuperscript{21} Accordingly, bearing no ill-will against their kinsmen [at Jerusalem], but rather remembering our connection with them, and the numerous matters with sincere heart from a remote period entrusted to them, we wished to venture a total alteration of their state, by bestowing upon them the rights of citizens of Alexandria, and to admit them to the everlasting rites of our solemnities.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{22} All this, however, they have taken in a very different spirit. With their innate malignity, they have spurned the fair offer; and constantly inclining to evil, \textsuperscript{23} have rejected the inestimable rights. Not only so, but by using speech, and by refraining from speech, they abhor the few among them who are heartily disposed towards us; ever deeming that their ignoble course of procedure will force us to do away with our reform. \textsuperscript{24} Having then, received certain proofs that these Jews bear us every sort of ill-will, we must look forward to the possibility of some sudden tumult among ourselves, when these impious men may turn traitors and barbarous enemies.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{25} As soon, therefore, as the contents of this letter become known to you, in that same hour we order those Jews who dwell among you, with wives and children, to be sent to us, vilified and abused, in chains of iron, to undergo a death, cruel and ignominious, suitable to men disaffected. \textsuperscript{26} For by the punishment of them in one body we perceive that we have found the only means of establishing our affairs for the future on a firm and satisfactory basis.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{27} Whoever shall shield a Jew, whether it be old man, child, or suckling, shall with his whole house be tortured to death. \textsuperscript{28} Whoever shall inform against the Jews , besides receiving the property of the person charged, shall be presented with two thousand drachmæ from the royal treasury, shall be made free, and shall be crowned.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{29} Whatever place shall shelter a Jew, shall, when he is hunted forth, be put under the ban of fire, and be for ever rendered useless to every living being for all time to come. \textsuperscript{30} Such was the purport of the king's letter.\par
\subsection*{Maccabees III 4}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} Wherever this decree was received, the people kept up a revelry of joy and shouting; as if their long-pent-up, hardened hatred, were now to shew itself openly.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{2} The Jews suffered great throes of sorrow, and wept much; while their hearts, all things around being lamentable, were set on fire as they bewailed the sudden destruction which was decreed against them. \textsuperscript{3} What home, or city, or place at all inhabited, or what streets were there, which their condition did not fill with wailing and lamentation?\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{4} They were sent out unanimously by the generals in the several cities, with such stern and pitiless feeling, that the exceptional nature of the infliction moved even some of their enemies. These, influenced by sentiments of common humanity, and reflecting upon the uncertain issue of life, shed tears at this their miserable expulsion. \textsuperscript{5} A multitude of aged hoary-haired men, were driven along with halting bending feet, urged onward by the impulse of a violent, shameless force to quick speed.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{6} Girls who had entered the bridal chamber quite lately, to enjoy the partnership of marriage, exchanged pleasure for misery; and with dust scattered upon their myrrh-anointed heads, were hurried along unveiled, and, in the midst of outlandish insults, set up with one accord a lamentable cry in lieu of the marriage hymn. \textsuperscript{7} Bound, and exposed to public gaze, they were hurried violently on board ship.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{8} The husbands of these, in the prime of their youthful vigour, instead of crowns wore halters round their necks; instead of feasting and youthful jollity, spent the rest of their nuptial days in wailings, and saw only the grave at hand. \textsuperscript{9} They were dragged along by unyielding chains, like wild beasts: of these, some had their necks thrust into the benches of the rowers; while the feet of others were enclosed in hard fetters. \textsuperscript{10} The planks of the deck above them barred out the light, and shut out the day on every side, so that they might be treated like traitors during the whole voyage.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{11} They were conveyed accordingly in this vessel, and at the end of it arrived at Schedia. The king had ordered them to be cast into the vast hippodrome, which was built in front of the city. This place was well adapted by its situation to expose them to the gaze of all comers into the city, and of those who went from the city into the country. Thus they could hold no communication with his forces; nay, were deemed unworthy of any civilized accommodation.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{12} When this was done, the king, hearing that their brethren in the city often went out and lamented the melancholy distress of these victims, \textsuperscript{13} was full of rage, and commanded that they should be carefully subjected to the same (and not one whit milder) treatment. \textsuperscript{14} The whole nation was now to be registered. Every individual was to be specified by name; not for that hard servitude of labour which we have a little before mentioned, but that he might expose them to the before-mentioned tortures; and finally, in the short space of a day, might extirpate them by his cruelties. \textsuperscript{15} The registering of these men was carried on cruelly, zealously, assiduously, from the rising of the sun to its going down, and was not brought to an end in forty days.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{16} The king was filled with great and constant joy, and celebrated banquets before the temple idols. His erring heart, far from the truth, and his profane mouth, gave glory to idols, deaf and incapable of speaking or aiding, and uttered unworthy speech against the Greatest God.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{17} At the end of the above-mentioned interval of time, the registrars brought word to the king that the multitude of the Jews was too great for registration, \textsuperscript{18} inasmuch as there were many still left in the land, of whom some were in inhabited houses, and others were scattered about in various places; so that all the commanders in Egypt were insufficient for the work. \textsuperscript{19} The king threatened them, and charged them with taking bribes, in order to contrive the escape of the Jews : but was clearly convinced of the truth of what had been said. \textsuperscript{20} They said, and proved, that paper and pens had failed them for the carrying out of their purpose. \textsuperscript{21} Now this was the active interference of the unconquerable Providence which assisted the Jews from heaven.\par
\subsection*{Maccabees III 5}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} Then he called Hermon, who had charge of the elephants. Full of rage, altogether fixed in his furious design, \textsuperscript{2} he commanded him, with a quantity of unmixed wine and handfuls of incense [infused] to drug the elephants early on the following day. These five hundred elephants were, when infuriated by the copious draughts of frankincense, to be led up to the execution of death upon the Jews. \textsuperscript{3} The king, after issuing these orders, went to his feasting, and gathered together all those of his friends and of the army who hated the Jews the most.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{4} The master of the elephants, Hermon, fulfilled his commission punctually. \textsuperscript{5} The underlings appointed for the purpose went out about eventide and bound the hands of the miserable victims, and took other precautions for their security at night, thinking that the whole race would perish together.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{6} The heathen believed the Jews to be destitute of all protection; for chains fettered them about. \textsuperscript{7} They invoked the Almighty Lord, and ceaselessly besought with tears their merciful God and Father, Ruler of all, Lord of every power, \textsuperscript{8} to overthrow the evil purpose which was gone out against them, and to deliver them by extraordinary manifestation from that death which was in store for them. \textsuperscript{9} Their litany so earnest went up to heaven.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{10} Then Hermon, who had filled his merciless elephants with copious draughts of mingled wine and frankincense, came early to the palace to certify the king thereof. \textsuperscript{11} He, however, who has sent his good creature sleep from all time, by night or by day thus gratifying whom he wills, diffused a portion thereof [now] upon the king. \textsuperscript{12} By this sweet and profound influence of the Lord he was held fast, and thus his unjust purpose was quite frustrated, and his unflinching resolve greatly falsified.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{13} But the Jews, having escaped the hour which had been fixed, praised their holy God, and again prayed him who is easily reconciled to display the power of his powerful hand to the overweening Gentiles. \textsuperscript{14} The middle of the tenth hour had well nigh arrived, when the master-bidder, seeing the guests who were bidden collected, came and shook the king. \textsuperscript{15} He gained his attention with difficulty, and hinting that the mealtime was getting past, talked the matter over with him.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{16} The king listened to this, and then turning aside to his potations, commanded the guests to sit down before him. \textsuperscript{17} This done, he asked them to enjoy themselves, and to indulge in mirth at this somewhat late hour of the banquet. \textsuperscript{18} Conversation grew on, and the king sent for Hermon, and enquired of him, with fierce denunciations, why the Jews had been allowed to outlive that day. \textsuperscript{19} Hermon explained that he had done his bidding over night; and in this he was confirmed by his friends. \textsuperscript{20} The king, then, with a barbarity exceeding that of Phalaris, said, That they might thank his sleep of that day. Lose no time, and get ready the elephants against to-morrow, as you did before, for the destruction of these accursed Jews.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{21} When the king said this, the company present were glad, and approved; and then each man went to his own home. \textsuperscript{22} Nor did they employ the night in sleep, so much as in contriving cruel mockeries for those deemed miserable.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{23} The morning cock had just crowed, and Hermon, having harnessed the brutes, was stimulating them in the great colonnade. \textsuperscript{24} The city crowds were collected together to see the hideous spectacle, and waited impatiently for the dawn. \textsuperscript{25} The Jews, breathless with momentary suspense, stretched forth their hands, and prayed the Greatest God, in mournful strains, again to help them speedily.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{26} The sun's rays were not yet shed abroad, and the king was waiting for his friends, when Hermon came to him, calling him out, and saying, That his desires could now be realized. \textsuperscript{27} The king, receiving him, was astonished at his unwonted exit; and, overwhelmed with a spirit of oblivion about everything, enquired the object of this earnest preparation. \textsuperscript{28} But this was the working of that Almighty God who had made him forget all his purpose.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{29} Hermon, and all his friends, pointed out the preparation of the animals. They are ready, O king, according to your own strict injunction. \textsuperscript{30} The king was filled with fierce anger at these words; for, by the Providence of God regarding these things, his mind had become entirely confused. He looked hard at Hermon, and threatened him as follows: \textsuperscript{31} Your parents, or your children, were they here, to these wild beasts a large repast they should have furnished; not these innocent Jews, who me and my forefathers loyally have served. \textsuperscript{32} Had it not been for familiar friendship, and the claims of your office, your life should have gone for theirs.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{33} Hermon, being threatened in this unexpected and alarming manner, was troubled in visage, and depressed in countenance. \textsuperscript{34} The friends, too, stole out one by one, and dismissed the assembled multitudes to their occupations. \textsuperscript{35} The Jews, having heard of these events, praised the glorious God and King of kings, because they had obtained this help, too, from him.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{36} Now the king arranged another banquet after the same manner, and proclaimed an invitation to mirth. \textsuperscript{37} And he summoned Hermon to his presence, and said, with threats, How often, O wretch, must I repeat my orders to thee about these same persons? \textsuperscript{38} Once more, arm the elephants against the morrow for the extermination of the Jews.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{39} His kinsmen, who were reclining with him, wondered at his instability, and thus expressed themselves: \textsuperscript{40} O king, how long dost thou make trial of us, as of men bereft of reason? This is the third time that thou hast ordered their destruction. When the thing is to be done, thou changest thy mind, and recallest thy instructions. \textsuperscript{41} For this cause the feeling of expectation causes tumult in the city: it swarms with factions; and is continually on the point of being plundered.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{42} The king, just like another Phalaris, a prey to thoughtlessness, made no account of the changes which his own mind had undergone, issuing in the deliverance of the Jews. He swore a fruitless oath, and determined forthwith to send them to Hades, crushed by the knees and feet of the elephants. \textsuperscript{43} He would also invade Judea, and level its towns with fire and the sword; and destroy that temple which the heathen might not enter, and prevent sacrifices ever after being offered up there.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{44} Joyfully his friends broke up, together with his kinsmen; and, trusting in his determination, arranged their forces in guard at the most convenient places of the city. \textsuperscript{45} And the master of the elephants urged the beasts into an almost maniacal state, drenched them with incense and wine, and decked them with frightful instruments.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{46} About early morning, when the city was now filled with an immense number of people at the hippodrome, he entered the palace, and called the king to the business in hand. \textsuperscript{47} The king's heart teemed with impious rage; and he rushed forth with the mass, along with the elephants. With feelings unsoftened, and eyes pitiless, he longed to gaze at the hard and wretched doom of the above-mentioned Jews .\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{48} But the Jews , when the elephants went out at the gate, followed by the armed force; and when they saw the dust raised by the throng, and heard the loud cries of the crowd, \textsuperscript{49} thought that they had come to the last moment of their lives, to the end of what they had tremblingly expected. They gave way, therefore, to lamentations and moans: they kissed each other: those nearest of kin to each other hung about one another's necks: fathers about their sons, mothers their daughters: other women held their infants to their breasts, which drew what seemed their last milk.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{50} Nevertheless, when they reflected upon the succour before granted them from heaven, they prostrated themselves with one accord; removed even the sucking children from the breast, and \textsuperscript{51} sent up an exceeding great cry, entreating the Lord of all power to reveal himself, and have mercy upon those who now lay at the gates of Hades.\par
\subsection*{Maccabees III 6}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} And Eleazar, an illustrious priest of the country, who had attained to length of days, and whose life had been adorned with virtue, caused the presbyters who were about him to cease to cry out to the holy God, and prayed thus:\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{2} O King, mighty in power, most high, Almighty God, who regulatest the whole creation with thy tender mercy, \textsuperscript{3} look upon the seed of Abraham, upon the children of the sanctified Jacob, thy sanctified inheritance, O Father, now being wrongfully destroyed as strangers in a strange land.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{4} Thou destroyedst Pharaoh, with his host of chariots, when that lord of this same Egypt was uplifted with lawless hardihood and loud-sounding tongue. Shedding the beams of thy mercy upon the race of Israel, thou didst overwhelm him with his proud army. \textsuperscript{5} When Sennacherim, the grievous king of the Assyrians, glorying in his countless hosts, had subdued the whole land with his spear, and was lifting himself against thy holy city, with boastings grievous to be endured, thou, O Lord, didst demolish him and didst shew forth thy might to many nations. \textsuperscript{6} When the three friends in the land of Babylon of their own will exposed their lives to the fire rather than serve vain things, thou didst send a dewy coolness through the fiery furnace, and bring the fire upon all their adversaries. \textsuperscript{7} It was thou who, when Daniel was hurled, through slander and envy, as a prey to lions down below, didst bring him back again unhurt to light. \textsuperscript{8} When Jonah was pining away in the belly of the sea-bred monster, thou didst look upon him, O Father, and recover him to the sight of his own.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{9} And now, thou who hatest insolence; thou who dost abound in mercy; thou who art the protector of all things; appear quickly to those of the race of Israel, who are insulted by abhorred, lawless Gentiles. \textsuperscript{10} If our life has during our exile been stained with iniquity, deliver us from the hand of the enemy, and destroy us, O Lord, by the death which thou preferrest.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{11} Let not the vain-minded congratulate vain idols at the destruction of thy beloved, saying, Neither did their God deliver them. \textsuperscript{12} Thou who art All-powerful and Almighty, O Eternal One, behold! have mercy upon us who are being withdrawn from life, like traitors, by the unreasoning insolence of lawless men. \textsuperscript{13} Let the heathen cower before thy invincible might to-day, O glorious One, who hast all power to save the race of Jacob. \textsuperscript{14} The whole band of infants and their parents with tears beseech thee. \textsuperscript{15} Let it be shewn to all the nations that thou art with us, O Lord, and hast not turned thy face away from us; but as thou saidst that thou wouldst not forget them even in the land of their enemies, so do thou fulfil this saying, O Lord.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{16} Now, at the time that Eleazar had ended his prayer, the king came along to the hippodrome, with the wild beasts, and with his tumultuous power. \textsuperscript{17} When the Jews saw this, they uttered a loud cry to heaven, so that the adjacent valleys resounded, and caused an irrepressible lamentation throughout the army.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{18} Then the all-glorious, all-powerful, and true God, displayed his holy countenance, and opened the gates of heaven, from which two angels, dreadful of form, came down, and were visible to all but the Jews. \textsuperscript{19} And they stood opposite, and filled the enemies' host with confusion and cowardice; and bound them with immoveable fetters. \textsuperscript{20} And a cold shudder came over the person of the king, and oblivion paralysed the vehemence of his spirit. \textsuperscript{21} They turned back the animals upon the armed forces which followed them; and the animals trod them down, and destroyed them.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{22} The king's wrath was converted into compassion; and he wept at his own machinations. \textsuperscript{23} For when he heard the cry, and saw them all on the verge of destruction, with tears he angrily threatened his friends, saying, \textsuperscript{24} Ye have governed badly; and have exceeded tyrants in cruelty; and me your benefactor ye have laboured to deprive at once of my dominion and my life, by secretly devising measures injurious to the kingdom. \textsuperscript{25} Who has gathered here, unreasonably removing each from his home, those who, in fidelity to us, had held the fortresses of the country? \textsuperscript{26} Who has thus consigned to unmerited punishments those who in good will towards us from the beginning have in all things surpassed all nations, and who often have engaged in the most dangerous undertakings?\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{27} Loose, loose the unjust bonds; send them to their homes in peace, and deprecate what has been done. \textsuperscript{28} Release the sons of the almighty living God of heaven, who from our ancestors' times until now has granted a glorious and uninterrupted prosperity to our affairs.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{29} These things he said: and they, released the same moment, having now escaped death, praised God their holy Saviour. \textsuperscript{30} The king then departed to the city, and called his financier to him, and bade him provide a seven days' quantity of wine and other materials for feasting for the Jews. He decided that they should keep a gladsome festival of deliverance in the very place in which they expected to meet with their destruction.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{31} Then they who were before despised and nigh unto Hades, yea, rather advanced into it, partook of the cup of salvation, instead of a grievous and lamentable death. Full of exultation, they parted out the place intended for their fall and burial into banqueting booths. \textsuperscript{32} Ceasing their miserable strain of woe, they took up the subject of their fatherland, hymning in praise God their wonder-working Saviour. All groans, all wailing, were laid aside: they formed dances in token of serene joy.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{33} So, also, the king collected a number of guests for the occasion, and returned unceasing thanks with much magnificence for the unexpected deliverance afforded him. \textsuperscript{34} Those who had marked them out as for death and for carrion, and had registered them with joy, howled aloud, and were clothed with shame, and had the fire of their rage ingloriously put out.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{35} But the Jews, as we just said, instituted a dance, and then gave themselves up to feasting, glad thanksgivings, and psalms. \textsuperscript{36} They made a public ordinance to commemorate these things for generations to come, as long as they should be sojourners. They thus established these days as days of mirth, not for the purpose of drinking or luxury, but because God had saved them. \textsuperscript{37} They requested the king to send them back to their homes.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{38} They were being enrolled from the twenty-fifth of Pachon to the fourth of Epiphi, a period of forty days: the measures taken for their destruction lasted from the fifth of Epiphi till the seventh, that is, three days. \textsuperscript{39} The Ruler over all did during this time manifest forth his mercy gloriously, and did deliver them all together unharmed.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{40} They feasted upon the king's provision up to the fourteenth day, and then asked to be sent away. \textsuperscript{41} The king commended them, and wrote the subjoined letter, of magnanimous import for them, to the commanders of every city.\par
\subsection*{Maccabees III 7}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} King Ptolemy Philopator to the commanders throughout Egypt, and to all who are set over affairs, joy and strength. \textsuperscript{2} We, too, and our children are well; and God has directed our affairs as we wish.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{3} Certain of our friends did of malice vehemently urge us to punish the Jews of our realm in a body, with the infliction of a monstrous punishment. \textsuperscript{4} They pretended that our affairs would never be in a good state till this took place. Such, they said, was the hatred borne by the Jews to all other people. \textsuperscript{5} They brought them fettered in grievous chains as slaves, nay, as traitors. Without enquiry or examination they endeavoured to annihilate them. They buckled themselves with a savage cruelty, worse than Scythian custom.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{6} For this cause we severely threatened them; yet, with the clemency which we are wont to extend to all men, we at length permitted them to live. Finding that the God of heaven cast a shield of protection over the Jews so as to preserve them, and that he fought for them as a father always fights for his sons; \textsuperscript{7} and taking into consideration their constancy and fidelity towards us and towards our ancestors, we have, as we ought, acquitted them of every sort of charge. \textsuperscript{8} And we have dismissed them to their several homes; bidding all men everywhere to do them no wrong, or unrighteously revile them about the past. \textsuperscript{9} For know ye, that should we conceive any evil design against, or in any manner aggrieve them, we shall ever have as our opposite, not man, but the highest God, the ruler of all might. From Him there will be no escape, as the avenger of such deeds. Fare ye well.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{10} When they had received this letter, they were not forward to depart immediately. They petitioned the king to be allowed to inflict fitting punishment upon those of their race who had willingly transgressed the holy God, and the law of God. \textsuperscript{11} They alleged that men who had for their bellies' sake transgressed the ordinances of God, would never be faithful to the interests of the king.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{12} The king admitted the truth of this reasoning, and commended them. Full power was given them, without warrant or special commission, to destroy those who had transgressed the law of God boldly in every part of the king's dominions. \textsuperscript{13} Their priests, then, as it was meet, saluted him with good wishes, and all the people echoed with the Hallelujah. They then joyfully departed.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{14} Then they punished and destroyed with ignominy every polluted Jew that fell in their way; \textsuperscript{15} slaying thus, in that day, above three hundred men, and esteeming this destruction of the wicked a season of joy. \textsuperscript{16} They themselves having held fast their God unto death, and having enjoyed a full deliverance, departed from the city garlanded with sweet-flowered wreaths of every kind. Uttering exclamations of joy, with songs of praise, and melodious hymns they thanked the God of their fathers, the eternal Saviour of Israel.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{17} Having arrived at Ptolemais, called from the specialty of that district Rose-bearing, where the fleet, in accordance with the general wish, waited for them seven days, \textsuperscript{18} they partook of a banquet of deliverance, for the king generously granted them severally the means of securing a return home. \textsuperscript{19} They were accordingly brought back in peace, while they gave utterance to becoming thanks; and they determined to keep these days during their sojourn as days of joyfulness. \textsuperscript{20} These they registered as sacred upon a pillar, when they had dedicated the place of their festivity to be one of prayer. They departed unharmed, free, abundant in joy, preserved by the king's command, by land, by sea, and by river, each to his own home.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{21} They had more weight than before among their enemies; and were honoured and feared, and no one in any way robbed them of their goods. \textsuperscript{22} Every man received back his own, according to inventory; those who had obtained their goods, giving them up with the greatest terror. For the greatest God wrought with perfectness wonders for their salvation. \textsuperscript{23} Blessed be the Redeemer of Israel unto everlasting. Amen.\par
\section*{Maccabees IV}
\subsection*{Maccabees IV 1}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} As I am going to demonstrate a most philosophical proposition, namely, that religious reasoning is absolute master of the passions, I would willingly advise you to give the utmost heed to philosophy. \textsuperscript{2} For reason is necessary to every one as a step to science: and more especially does it embrace the praise of prudence, the highest virtue.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{3} If, then, reasoning appears to hold the mastery over the passions which stand in the way of temperance, such as gluttony and lust, \textsuperscript{4} it surely also and manifestly has the rule over the affections which are contrary to justice, such as malice; and of those which are hindrances to manliness, as wrath, and pain, and fear. \textsuperscript{5} How, then, is it, perhaps some may say, that reasoning, if it rule the affections, is not also master of forgetfulness and ignorance? They attempt a ridiculous argument. \textsuperscript{6} For reasoning does not rule over its own affections, but over such as are contrary to justice, and manliness, and temperance, and prudence; and yet over these, so as to withstand, without destroying them.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{7} I might prove to you, from many other considerations, that religious reasoning is sole master of the passions; \textsuperscript{8} but I shall prove it with the greatest force from the fortitude of Eleazar, and seven brethren, and their mother, who suffered death in defence of virtue. \textsuperscript{9} For all these, contemning pains even unto death, by this contempt, demonstrated that reasoning has command over the passions.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{10} For their virtues, then, it is right that I should commend those men who died with their mother at this time in behalf of rectitude; and for their honours, I may count them happy. \textsuperscript{11} For they, winning admiration not only from men in general, but even from their persecutors, for their manliness and endurance, became the means of the destruction of the tyranny against their nation, having conquered the tyrant by their endurance, so that by them their country was purified.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{12} But we may now at once enter upon the question, having commenced, as is our wont, with laying down the doctrine, and so proceed to the account of these persons, giving glory to the all wise God.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{13} The question, therefore, is, whether reasoning be absolute master of the passions. \textsuperscript{14} Let us determine, then, What is reasoning? and what passion? and how many forms of the passions? and whether reasoning bears sway over all of these?\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{15} Reasoning is, then, intellect accompanied by a life of rectitude, putting foremost the consideration of wisdom. \textsuperscript{16} And wisdom is a knowledge of divine and human things, and of their causes. \textsuperscript{17} And this is contained in the education of the law; by means of which we learn divine things reverently, and human things profitably.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{18} And the forms of wisdom are prudence, and justice, and manliness, and temperance. \textsuperscript{19} The leading one of these is prudence; by whose means, indeed, it is that reasoning bears rule over the passions. \textsuperscript{20} Of the passions, pleasure and pain are the two most comprehensive; and they also by nature refer to the soul. \textsuperscript{21} And there are many attendant affections surrounding pleasure and pain. \textsuperscript{22} Before pleasure is lust; and after pleasure, joy. \textsuperscript{23} And before pain is fear; and after pain, sorrow.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{24} Wrath is an affection, common to pleasure and to pain, if any one will pay attention when it comes upon him. \textsuperscript{25} And there exists in pleasure a malicious disposition, which is the most multiform of all the affections. \textsuperscript{26} In the soul it is arrogance, and love of money, and vaingloriousness, and contention, and faithlessness, and the evil eye. \textsuperscript{27} In the body it is greediness and gormandizing, and solitary gluttony.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{28} As pleasure and pain are, therefore, two growths of the body and the soul, so there are many offshoots of these passions. \textsuperscript{29} And reasoning, the universal husbandman, purging, and pruning these severally, and binding round, and watering, and transplanting, in every way improves the materials of the morals and affections. \textsuperscript{30} For reasoning is the leader of the virtues, but it is the sole ruler of the passions. Observe then first, through the very things which stand in the way of temperance, that reasoning is absolute ruler of the passions.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{31} Now temperance consists of a command over the lusts. \textsuperscript{32} But of the lusts, some belong to the soul, others to the body: and over each of these classes the reasoning appears to bear sway. \textsuperscript{33} For whence is it, otherwise, that when urged on to forbidden meats, we reject the gratification which would ensue from them? Is it not because reasoning is able to command the appetites? I believe so. \textsuperscript{34} Hence it is, then, that when lusting after water-animals and birds, and fourfooted beasts, and all kinds of food which are forbidden us by the law, we withhold ourselves through the mastery of reasoning. \textsuperscript{35} For the affections of our appetites are resisted by the temperate understanding, and bent back again, and all the impulses of the body are reined in by reasoning.\par
\subsection*{Maccabees IV 2}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} And what wonder? if the lusts of the soul, after participation with what is beautiful, are frustrated, \textsuperscript{2} on this ground, therefore, the temperate Joseph is praised in that by reasoning, he subdued, on reflection, the indulgence of sense. \textsuperscript{3} For, although young, and ripe for sexual intercourse, he abrogated by reasoning the stimulus of his passions.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{4} And it is not merely the stimulus of sensual indulgence, but that of every desire, that reasoning is able to master. \textsuperscript{5} For instance, the law says, Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor anything that belongs to thy neighbour. \textsuperscript{6} Now, then, since it is the law which has forbidden us to desire, I shall much the more easily persuade you, that reasoning is able to govern our lusts, just as it does the affections which are impediments to justice. \textsuperscript{7} Since in what way is a solitary eater, and a glutton, and a drunkard reclaimed, unless it be clear that reasoning is lord of the passions?\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{8} A man, therefore, who regulates his course by the law, even if he be a lover of money, straightway puts force upon his own disposition; lending to the needy without interest, and cancelling the debt of the incoming sabbath. \textsuperscript{9} And should a man be parsimonious, he is ruled by the law acting through reasoning; so that he does not glean his harvest crops, nor vintage: and in reference to other points we may perceive that it is reasoning that conquers his passions.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{10} For the law conquers even affection toward parents, not surrendering virtue on their account. \textsuperscript{11} And it prevails over marriage love, condemning it when transgressing law. \textsuperscript{12} And it lords it over the love of parents toward their children, for they punish them for vice; and it domineers over the intimacy of friends, reproving them when wicked. \textsuperscript{13} And think it not a strange assertion that reasoning can in behalf of the law conquer even enmity. \textsuperscript{14} It alloweth not to cut down the cultivated herbage of an enemy, but preserveth it from the destroyers, and collecteth their fallen ruins.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{15} And reasoning appears to be master of the more violent passions, as love of empire and empty boasting, and arrogance, and loud boasting, and slander. \textsuperscript{16} For the temperate understanding repels all these malignant passions, as it does wrath: for it masters even this.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{17} Thus Moses, when angered against Dathan and Abiram, did nothing to them in wrath, but regulated his anger by reasoning. \textsuperscript{18} For the temperate mind is able, as I said, to be superior to the passions, and to transfer some, and destroy others. \textsuperscript{19} For why, else, does our most wise father Jacob blame Simeon and Levi for having irrationally slain the whole race of the Shechemites, saying, Cursed be their anger. \textsuperscript{20} For if reasoning did not possess the power of subduing angry affections, he would not have spoken thus.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{21} For at the time when God created man, He implanted within him his passions and moral nature. \textsuperscript{22} And at that time He enthroned above all the holy leader mind, through the medium of the senses. \textsuperscript{23} And He gave a law to this mind , by living according to which it will maintain a temperate, and just, and good, and manly reign. \textsuperscript{24} How, then, a man may say, if reasoning be master of the passions, has it no control over forgetfulness and ignorance?\par
\subsection*{Maccabees IV 3}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} The argument is exceedingly ridiculous: for reasoning does not appear to bear sway over its own affections, but over those of the body, \textsuperscript{2} in such a way as that any one of you may not be able to root out desire, but reasoning will enable you to avoid being enslaved to it.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{3} One may not be able to root out anger from the soul, but it is possible to withstand anger. \textsuperscript{4} Any one of you may not be able to eradicate malice, but reasoning has force to work with you to prevent your yielding to malice. \textsuperscript{5} For reasoning is not an eradicator, but an antagonist of the passions. \textsuperscript{6} And this may be more clearly comprehended from the thirst of King David. \textsuperscript{7} For after David had been attacking the Philistines the whole day, he with the soldiers of his nation slew many of them; \textsuperscript{8} then when evening came, sweating and very weary, he came to the royal tent, about which the entire host of our ancestors was encamped.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{9} Now all the rest of them were at supper; \textsuperscript{10} but the king, being very much athirst, although he had numerous springs, could not by their means quench his thirst; \textsuperscript{11} but a certain irrational longing for the water in the enemy's camp grew stronger and fiercer upon him, and consumed him with languish.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{12} Wherefore his body-guards being troubled at this longing of the king, two valiant young soldiers, reverencing the desire of the king, put on their panoplies, and taking a pitcher, got over the ramparts of the enemies: \textsuperscript{13} and unperceived by the guardians of the gate, they went throughout the whole camp of the enemy in quest. \textsuperscript{14} And having boldly discovered the fountain, they filled out of it the draught for the king.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{15} But he, though parched up with thirst, reasoned that a draught reputed of equal value to blood, would be terribly dangerous to his soul. \textsuperscript{16} Wherefore, setting up reasoning in opposition to his desire, he poured out the draught to God. \textsuperscript{17} For the temperate mind has power to conquer the pressure of the passions, and to quench the fires of excitement, \textsuperscript{18} and to wrestle down the pains of the body, however excessive; and, through the excellency of reasoning, to abominate all the assaults of the passions.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{19} But the occasion now invites us to give an illustration of temperate reasoning from history. \textsuperscript{20} For at a time when our fathers were in possession of undisturbed peace through obedience to the law, and were prosperous, so that Seleucus Nicanor, the king of Asia, both assigned them money for divine service, and accepted their form of government, \textsuperscript{21} then certain persons, bringing in new things contrary to the general unanimity, in various ways fell into calamities.\par
\subsection*{Maccabees IV 4}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} For a certain man named Simon, who was in opposition to Onias, who once held the high priesthood for life, and was an honourable and good man, after that by slandering him in every way, he could not injure him with the people, went away as an exile, with the intention of betraying his country.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{2} Whence coming to Apollonius, the military governor of Syria, and Phœnicia, and Cilicia, he said, \textsuperscript{3} Having good will to the king's affairs, I am come to inform thee that infinite private wealth is laid up in the treasuries of Jerusalem which do not belong to the temple, but pertain to king Seleucus.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{4} Apollonius, acquainting himself with the particulars of this, praised Simon for his care of the king's interests, and going up to Seleucus informed him of the treasure; \textsuperscript{5} and getting authority about it, and quickly advancing into our country with the accursed Simon and a very heavy force, \textsuperscript{6} he said that he came with the commands of the king that he should take the private money of the treasury. \textsuperscript{7} And the nation, indignant at this proclamation, and replying to the effect that it was extremely unfair that those who had committed deposits to the sacred treasury should be deprived of them, resisted as well as they could. \textsuperscript{8} But Apollonius went away with threats into the temple.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{9} And the priests, with the women and children, having supplicated God to throw his shield over the holy, despised place, \textsuperscript{10} and Apollonius going up with his armed force to the seizure of the treasure,—there appeared from heaven angels riding on horseback, all radiant in armour, filling them with much fear and trembling. \textsuperscript{11} And Apollonius fell down half dead upon the court which is open to all nations, and extended his hands to heaven, and implored the Hebrews, with tears, to pray for him, and propitiate the heavenly host. \textsuperscript{12} For he said that he had sinned, so as to be consequently worthy of death; and that if he were saved, he would celebrate to all men the blessedness of the holy place.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{13} Onias the high priest, induced by these words, although for other reasons anxious that king Seleucus should not suppose that Apollonius was slain by human device and not by Divine punishment, prayed for him; \textsuperscript{14} and he being thus unexpectedly saved, departed to manifest to the king what had happened to him.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{15} But on the death of Seleucus the king, his son Antiochus Epiphanes succeeds to the kingdom: a man of haughty pride and terrible. \textsuperscript{16} Who having deposed Onias from the high priesthood, appointed his brother Jason to be high priest: \textsuperscript{17} who had made a covenant, if he would give him this authority, to pay yearly three thousand six hundred and sixty talents.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{18} And he committed to him the high priesthood and rulership over the nation. \textsuperscript{19} And he both changed the manner of living of the people, and perverted their civil customs into all lawlessness. \textsuperscript{20} So that he not only erected a gymnasium on the very citadel of our country, [but neglected] the guardianship of the temple. \textsuperscript{21} At which Divine vengeance being grieved, instigated Antiochus himself against them. \textsuperscript{22} For being at war with Ptolemy in Egypt, he heard that on a report of his death being spread abroad, the inhabitants of Jerusalem had exceedingly rejoiced, and he quickly marched against them. \textsuperscript{23} And having subdued them, he established a decree that if any of them lived according to the laws of his country, he should die.\par
\noindent \textsuperscript{24} And when he could by no means destroy by his decrees the obedience to the law of the nation, but saw all his threats and punishments without effect, \textsuperscript{25} for even women, because they continued to circumcise their children, were flung down a precipice along with them, knowing beforehand of the punishment. \textsuperscript{26} When, therefore, his decrees were disregarded by the people, he himself compelled by means of tortures every one of this race, by tasting forbidden meats, to abjure the Jewish religion.\par
\subsection*{Maccabees IV 5}
\noindent \textsuperscript{1} The tyrant Antiochus, therefore, sitting in public state with his assessors upon a certain lofty place, with his armed troops standing in a circle round him, \textsuperscript{2} commanded his spearbearers to seize every one of the Hebrews, and to compel them to taste swine's flesh, and things offered to idols. \textsuperscript{3} And should any of them be unwilling to eat the accursed food, they were to be tortured on the wheel, and so killed.\par
